title: How a leader influences team performance
blurb: Explain the levers a project team leader pulls to raise performance, and the behaviours that drag it down.
question: A software team's output has dropped for three sprints. The members are capable, but they say priorities keep changing, nobody notices good work and they wait days for decisions. How can the team leader influence performance?

teach.h: The leader is the biggest lever on performance
teach.body: The same people can deliver brilliantly or poorly depending on how they are led. A project team leader influences performance by what they set (vision and objectives), how they treat people (motivation, recognition, feedback, trust, wellbeing), what they enable (empowerment, resources, removing obstacles, resolving conflict) and how they behave themselves (leading by example, adapting their style). Every one of these either lifts the team or holds it back.

teach.h: The leader's levers, in four groups
teach.caption: Twelve levers. Exam options that name any of these are describing positive leader influence.

teach.h: Lever and its effect on the team
head: Leader action
Effect on performance

steps.label:
Good work
done
steps.sub: A member solves a tricky defect

steps.label: Noticed
steps.sub: The leader sees and names it

teach.caption: Recognition that is specific and timely makes good behaviour more likely to be repeated across the team.

teach.h: Adapt your style to the team
teach.body: No single leadership style suits every situation. A new or unsure team needs clear direction; a team in conflict needs coaching and help to resolve it; a settled team needs support; a mature, high-performing team needs the leader to delegate and step back. Adapting style to the situation and the team's stage of development gives people the right amount of direction and support, so they neither flounder nor feel smothered.

teach.h: Behaviours that lift or drag performance

teach.body: Dev leads a team building a ferry-booking app. Output has fallen for three sprints. In one-to-ones he hears that the test environment keeps failing, priorities change daily and good work goes unnoticed. He secures a stable test environment from IT, agrees a fixed sprint goal with the product owner, starts naming specific contributions at each review and lets the developers choose how to split the work. Within two sprints output has recovered.

teach.caption: Listening, honesty and fairness build trust; trust means problems surface while they are still small.

teach.text: Exam distractors offer actions that feel like control but lower performance: supervising every task closely, making all decisions personally, avoiding conflict to keep the peace, or only giving feedback at the end of the project. The right answer usually involves clarity, recognition, coaching, trust or removing obstacles.

items: Direction: clear vision and objectives, effective communication, involving the team in decisions.
People: motivation and recognition, feedback and coaching, trust and a positive culture, wellbeing.
Enabling: empowering and delegating, removing obstacles and securing resources, managing conflict.
Self: lead by example and adapt your style to the situation and the team's stage.

summary: You can now explain how a project team leader influences performance through direction, the way they treat people, what they enable and how they behave. You can also spot the controlling or avoiding behaviours that look busy but drag a team's performance down.

A.q: Which leader behaviour is most likely to improve a project team's performance?
options: Checking every task before it is released
Making all key decisions without the team
Setting clear objectives the team agrees to
Leaving the team to discover the priorities
A.why: Clear, agreed objectives give the team focus and a shared direction, which improves performance.

whyNot.0: Checking every task is micromanagement; it slows work and signals lack of trust.
whyNot.1: Excluding the team from decisions reduces ownership and commitment.
whyNot.3: Unclear priorities waste effort and cause confusion.

A.q: A team leader thanks a member at the sprint review for a specific piece of work. How is this most likely to affect performance?
options: It raises morale and encourages repetition
It makes the rest of the team less engaged
It has no effect, as pay drives performance
It creates confusion about who is accountable
A.why: Specific, timely recognition boosts morale and makes the recognised behaviour more likely to be repeated.

whyNot.1: Fair, specific recognition generally motivates the wider team rather than disengaging them.
whyNot.2: Recognition is a powerful motivator in its own right, not just pay.
whyNot.3: Thanking someone for their work does not change who is accountable for it.

A.q: Which TWO of the following are ways a leader can positively influence team performance? 1. Leading by example  2. Withholding information  3. Coaching team members  4. Avoiding all conflict
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
A.why: Leading by example (1) sets the standard and coaching (3) builds capability and confidence.

whyNot.0: Withholding information (2) stops people making good decisions.
whyNot.1: Withholding information (2) and avoiding conflict (4) both harm performance.
whyNot.2: Avoiding conflict (4) lets problems grow; conflict should be managed early and fairly.

B.q: Two members keep clashing over how a design should be done and the work has stalled. What should the leader do to protect performance?
options: Ignore it and hope they settle in time
Address it promptly, openly and fairly
Remove both people from the project
Side with whoever is the more senior
B.why: Managing conflict promptly and fairly restores focus and co-operation, protecting performance.

whyNot.0: Ignored conflict tends to grow and spread, damaging the whole team.
whyNot.2: Removing both people is drastic and loses their skills; the conflict can usually be resolved.
whyNot.3: Siding by seniority is unfair and damages trust in the leader.

B.q: Complete the statement: a leader who removes obstacles and secures the resources the team needs mainly helps the team to…
options: avoid reporting progress to the sponsor
work without any agreed objectives
keep momentum and work effectively
take over the leader's own decisions
B.why: Clearing blockers and securing resources lets the team keep moving and work effectively.

whyNot.0: Reporting to the sponsor still happens; removing obstacles is not about avoiding it.
whyNot.1: Objectives are still needed; removing obstacles helps the team achieve them.
whyNot.3: Clearing obstacles supports the team; it does not hand over the leader's decisions.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a way a leader positively influences team performance?
options: Involving the team in decisions
Supporting the team's wellbeing
Supervising every task in detail
Building trust and a good culture
B.why: Close supervision of every task is micromanagement; it undermines trust and ownership and slows the team.

whyNot.0: Involving the team in decisions builds ownership and commitment.
whyNot.1: Supporting wellbeing helps people sustain their effort.
whyNot.3: Trust and a positive culture help problems surface early and improve results.

C.q: A project manager leads a team of experienced engineers who now work well together and need little supervision. Which approach will best maintain their performance?
options: Delegate and give them autonomy
Give detailed daily instructions
Restart team-building from day one
Make every decision on their behalf
C.why: A mature, capable team performs best when the leader adapts style by delegating and giving autonomy.

whyNot.1: Detailed instructions suit a new, unsure team; here they would frustrate capable people.
whyNot.2: Starting team-building again is unnecessary for a team already working well together.
whyNot.3: Making all decisions removes the ownership that drives a mature team.

C.q: A team leader gives a struggling member regular, specific feedback and pairs them with an experienced colleague. Which lever is the leader mainly using?
options: Securing extra resources
Feedback and coaching
Managing team conflict
Setting the team vision
C.why: Specific feedback plus guided support from a colleague is feedback and coaching, which builds capability and confidence.

whyNot.0: No new resources have been secured; the leader is developing an existing member.
whyNot.2: There is no conflict described; the member is struggling with the work.
whyNot.3: The vision is about where the project is going, not one person's development.

C.q: A leader insists on punctual, well-prepared meetings but regularly arrives late and unprepared. What is the most likely effect on the team?
options: Standards rise because the rule is clear
Accountability for meetings becomes clearer
No effect, because the rule is written down
Standards slip because the example is poor
C.why: People copy what a leader does more than what they say; a poor example undermines the standard.

whyNot.0: A clear rule has little force when the leader visibly ignores it.
whyNot.1: Inconsistent behaviour blurs accountability rather than clarifying it.
whyNot.2: Written rules do not outweigh the example set by the leader's behaviour.

reteach.title: Think of a kitchen brigade
reteach.question: Two restaurants have equally skilled chefs. One kitchen hums; the other is chaos. What is the head chef doing differently?

blocks.body: In the calm kitchen, the head chef briefs everyone on tonight's menu (direction), trusts each section to run its station (delegation), tastes and gives quick, specific feedback (coaching), fixes the broken oven before service (removing obstacles), stays calm under pressure (leading by example) and thanks the team at the end (recognition). In the chaotic kitchen, the head chef shouts orders, does everything personally and only speaks up when something goes wrong.

blocks.text: Doing everything yourself and checking every task is not strong leadership. It slows the team and kills ownership. Influence comes from clarity, trust, coaching and support.

explain.body: A clear vision and objectives tell people what success looks like. Effective communication keeps everyone informed, and involving the team in decisions builds ownership of the result.

test.q: How does involving the team in decisions most often influence performance?
options: It slows every decision, so output falls
It removes the need for any objectives
It shifts accountability to the sponsor
It builds ownership of the outcome
test.why: People who help shape decisions feel ownership of them and commit more fully to delivering them.

whyNot.0: Involvement can take a little time but usually improves commitment and output overall.
whyNot.1: Objectives are still needed; involvement helps people commit to them.
whyNot.2: Involving the team does not move accountability to the sponsor.

explain.body: Motivation and recognition, regular feedback and coaching, trust and a positive culture, and support for wellbeing all help people want to give their best and keep doing so over the life of the project.

test.q: Which leader action most directly builds trust within a team?
options: Listening and acting on concerns
Keeping decisions to themselves
Changing priorities without notice
Praising only the top performers
test.why: Listening and then acting on what people raise shows respect and reliability, which builds trust.

whyNot.1: Secrecy over decisions breeds suspicion, not trust.
whyNot.2: Unexplained changes make the leader seem unpredictable.
whyNot.3: Praising only a few seems unfair and can damage trust in the wider team.

explain.body: Empowering and delegating gives people authority to act. Removing obstacles and securing resources keeps them moving. Managing conflict promptly and fairly stops disagreements from draining the team's energy.

test.q: How does appropriate delegation most often influence a team's performance?
options: It reduces their sense of ownership
It increases ownership and motivation
It removes the leader's accountability
It means objectives are no longer needed
test.why: Delegating authority with trust increases ownership and motivation, improving output.

whyNot.0: Delegation increases ownership rather than reducing it.
whyNot.2: The leader remains accountable even when work is delegated.
whyNot.3: Delegated work still needs clear objectives.

explain.body: Leaders influence through their own behaviour: people copy what they see. They also adapt their style to the situation and the team's stage of development, giving more direction to a new team and more freedom to a mature one.

test.q: Why should a leader adapt their style to the team's needs and maturity?
options: So that every team is treated the same
So the leader can avoid making decisions
To give the right direction and support
To reduce the amount of communication
test.why: Matching style to the team gives the right level of direction and support, keeping the team effective.

whyNot.0: Treating every team identically ignores their differing needs, which is the opposite of adapting.
whyNot.1: Adapting style is not a way to avoid decisions.
whyNot.3: Adapting style does not mean communicating less.
